A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same CCS research. All 13 pages of v2 and 16 pages of v3, including appendices, tables, equations, and figures, support comparison. Reporting inconsistencies do not prevent identifying the changes.

before.justification: v2 reports original pruning experiments on classification, video retrieval, and social bias, together with human–LLM agreement results and analyses of attention-head concepts.

after.justification: v3 retains these empirical results and adds description-count sensitivity, equal-count pruning, low-CCS bias comparisons, and concept-redundancy analysis.

M1.justification: The core procedure remains TEXTSPAN extraction, ChatGPT concept labeling, unanimous assessment by three LLM judges, CCS categorization, and soft pruning. The description-count experiments vary an evaluation setting; the new CCR metric analyzes existing heads without changing the proposed pruning procedure.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same classification, OOD, video-retrieval, and bias datasets. The added sensitivity and equal-count experiments reuse existing datasets, while Appendix B analyzes existing model heads rather than introducing new task coverage.

E2.justification: v3 adds low-CCS pruning as a comparator in both bias experiments: v2 Tables 7–8 compare only original and high-CCS-pruned models, whereas v3 Tables 8–9 include low-CCS columns. Comparator membership in the retained classification and retrieval comparisons is unchanged.

E3.justification: v3 substantially expands the evaluation design with TEXTSPAN counts of 5, 7, 9, 11, and 13; equal-count high/low-CCS pruning on three datasets; and modelwise and layerwise CCR evaluation. These are additional protocols, not demonstrated revisions to the retained experiments. Existing accuracy, retrieval, and MaxSkew metrics remain unchanged.

E4.justification: New Section 3.4 tests sensitivity to description count, expanded Section 4.2 tests whether pruning-count imbalance explains performance differences, and Appendix B investigates conceptual redundancy and layerwise duplication. These substantially extend the original robustness and mechanism analyses.

E5.justification: Both versions average random pruning over five seeds/runs and retain the same human–LLM agreement statistics. v3 introduces no additional uncertainty-reporting practice, confidence intervals, error bars, significance tests, or documented increase in repeated runs.

E6.justification: v3 adds sensitivity, equal-count, CCR, and low-CCS bias results while retaining the earlier classification and retrieval scores. Existing bias results also change beyond rounding: original/high-CCS values exchange race/gender assignments in the first two SocialCounterFactuals rows, and ViT-L-14-OpenAI high-pruned gender changes from 1.62 to 2.0 (v2 Table 8; v3 Table 9). FairFace datacomp original gender changes from 21.35 to 21.7.

T1.justification: Appendix B introduces the mathematical definition CCR = Cmulti/Hhigh to quantify concepts shared by multiple high-CCS heads. This is a limited formal addition; the CCS and CCS@K definitions remain unchanged, and no theorem or proof development is added.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same principal contributions: CCS identifies important concept-aligned heads, these heads support classification and retrieval, and pruning them exposes a performance–bias tradeoff. The rewritten abstract and additional supporting analyses do not redefine these central claims.

C2.justification: v3 newly argues that CCS is insensitive to description count, that matched pruning rules out head-count confounding, and that distributed representations better explain resilience than layerwise duplication. Section 6 adds limitations concerning transfer beyond CLIP and manual verification/scaling of LLM judgments. It also removes v2’s contrastive-learning explanation of how high-CCS heads acquire social biases.

D1.justification: Section 3.1 newly specifies the image encoder and documents an inherited pool of 3,498 descriptions generated using ChatGPT-3.5 with manual prompting for additional patterns. This expands provenance disclosure without establishing changed underlying inputs. Existing head lists and occupation prompts remain available.

R1.justification: v3 adds five cited works, including Abnar and Zuidema, Barkan, Shu, Mayilvahanan, and Moeller, with limited new positioning against descriptive attention interpretation and CLIP generalization research. The broader related-work narrative and dependence on TEXTSPAN remain intact.

P1.justification: The abstract is rewritten, author spelling and affiliations are updated, and local methodological explanations are expanded. New sensitivity, limitations, and appendix headings extend the structure, but most existing prose and the overall section sequence remain unchanged.

P2.justification: v3 adds head-count, sensitivity, equal-count, and CCR tables; expands both bias tables; and moves occupation/prompt tables into the appendix. Figures 2–5 receive revised sizing and labels, with a tighter vertical range in Figure 4. Typography, spacing, headers, and float placement are extensively reformatted. The head-count table summarizes previously listed heads.

improvement.justification: v3 adds useful provenance, limitations, and potentially valuable controls. However, Section 4.2 contradicts Table 7: matched high-CCS pruning gives 62.39 versus 58.58 for low-CCS pruning on ViT-B-32-OpenAI/CIFAR-100, despite claiming greater damage from high-CCS pruning. Table 3 also shows 63.93–76.74 for ViT-B-16-OpenAI/CIFAR-10 across description counts, weakening the asserted stability. These conflicts and unexplained bias-result reassignments leave the evidential benefits of the additions unresolved, preventing a reliable net quality judgment.
